comment.value:
This paper proposes a dataset distillation framework for 3D point clouds based on distribution matching. It introduces a Semantically Aligned Distribution Matching (SADM) module to resolve misaligned semantic structures across different models. Additionally, it incorporates learnable rotation parameters to handle intra-class variability arising from different acquisition poses. The reviewers unanimously gave positive feedback. The paper makes a novel contribution by jointly optimizing dataset distillation with semantic alignment and learnable rotations, effectively addressing key limitations of existing methods. 

Recommendation: Accept. The AC valued this paper and suggested cross-dataset evaluation and suggested additional experiments confirming the method’s superiority.

We would like to express our gratitude to the Area Chair for coordinating the
review process of our paper. We also thank all reviewers again for their time
and constructive feedback, which greatly improved the clarity and completeness
of our paper. The following is a summary of the discussion between the authors
and the reviewers regarding the authors’ rebuttal.


- **Reviewer 66sg** acknowledged the originality and significance of our paper
and stated that our rebuttal addressed the reviewer’s concerns. Finally,
the reviewer further raised the evaluation score in support of our paper’s
acceptance.
- **Reviewer ZBoM** highlighted the strengths of our proposed semantically
and rotationally aligned matching algorithm and stated that our rebuttal
resolved most of the confusion. Finally, the reviewer decided to raise the
evaluation score to support the acceptance of our paper.
- **Reviewer H221** recognized that our paper leverages the unique properties of point clouds to perform dataset distillation and stated that our rebuttal addressed some of the concerns. This reviewer still commented that
cross-dataset evaluation could better reflect generalizability. We replied
to this comment why the cross-architecture evaluation is commonly used
in dataset distillation research; nevertheless, in response to the reviewer’s
comment, we conducted additional experiments of cross-dataset evaluation. The results confirmed that the proposed method still outperforms
existing approaches. However, we did not receive any further comments
from the reviewer regarding this issue.
- **Reviewer WfS3** acknowledged the novelty of our work in addressing a
relatively new problem of dataset distillation for point clouds and stated
that our rebuttal addressed most of the reviewer’s concerns. Finally, the
reviewer raised the evaluation score leaning toward the acceptance of our
paper.


We are encouraged that all reviewers acknowledged our contributions, with several ratings increased after the rebuttal. We believe that our work provides a
foundation for future research in the efficient learning of 3D point clouds.

Specifically, we used the 16 classes shared between ShapeNet and ModelNet40, and performed the following two settings:

Dear reviewer H221,

Thank you for careful reading our rebuttal and valuable comment on generalizability.

The dataset distillation aims to generate a distilled dataset that exhibits similar behavior to the original dataset. From this perspective, we respectfully clarify that our purpose is to evaluate the generalizability of **DISTILLED DATASET** itself, not the generalizability of **MODEL**. The cross-dataset experiment evaluates the generalizability of **MODEL**, whereas cross-architecture evaluation focus on that of **DISTILLED DATASET**. For this reason, all the existing literatures of dataset distillation research, e.g., [3, 28,29], always adopt the cross-architecture evaluation to evaluate the generalizability, as it demonstrates how well the distilled dataset generalizes to unseen model architectures. We sincerely hope that this explanation has been helpful in addressing your concern.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the novelty of our work in addressing the relatively new problem of dataset distillation for point clouds. We respond to the reviewer's comments as follows.   

**Q1: Significance of the proposed method**

Table 1 provides the comparison of quantitative performance at the same PPC (point clouds per class). 'Whole' refers to the classification accuracy obtained by training the network on the entire original dataset without any distillation. It serves as an upper bound for evaluating the performance drop introduced by using reduced (distilled) datasets. 'Ratio(\%)' represents the percentage of the distilled dataset size compared to that of the entire original dataset. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves the performance compared with the existing methodologies, that means our distilled dataset preserves more useful information than the other methods. Furthermore, Table 2 reports the cross-architecture generalization results, in which our proposed method consistently outperforms existing approaches by substantial margins, reinforcing the claim that it effectively retains useful information. We will discuss and reflect this in more detail in the experiments section.


**Q2: Comparison with other image dataset distillation methods**

The dataset distillation for 3D point clouds remains a largely unexplored research area, with PCC [27] being the only existing method introduced thus far. With respect to the comparison against image-based dataset distillation methods, we would like to highlight that our paper already presents comprehensive experimental results. Section 4.2 and Table 1 in the main paper provided the comparative results with DC [29] of gradient matching and DM [28] of distribution matching. In addition, Table 4 in the supplementary material also provided comparative experimental results with MTT [3] of trajectory matching and DataDAM [17] of another distribution matching-based method. We present these results again in the table below. Notably, all experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms both representative image dataset distillation methods across various datasets and PPC settings.

We thank the reviewer to acknowledge our effort to leverage the unique properties of point clouds to perform dataset distillation. We respond to the reviewer's comments as follows.

**Q1: Related work refinement**

We appreciate the reviewer for the feedback on the Related Works section. Section 2.1 introduces point cloud analysis methods to clarify which architectures are used in our framework. Specifically, PointNet serves as the backbone architecture in our dataset distillation pipeline, while the other architectures are used as evaluation networks in our cross-architecture generalization experiments (Table 2). Section 2.2 discusses coreset selection methods, which were widely used before the emergence of dataset distillation. These methods share the same objective of reducing training data size while preserving model performance, but they achieve this by selecting real samples rather than generating synthetic ones. Since they operate solely within the space of existing samples, they lack the flexibility to represent rare or task-specific patterns. We compare against these methods in Table 1 to highlight the advantages of distillation-based approaches. Section 2.3 covers recent dataset distillation techniques, including gradient matching, trajectory matching, and distribution matching. These methods are parallel to ours in their goal of synthesizing informative datasets, but they are primarily designed for image data. Applying them to 3D point clouds is non-trivial due to challenges such as the unordered nature of point cloud data and its sensitivity to rotational variance. While PCC~[27] is the only existing method designed for 3D point clouds, it directly adopts an image-based gradient matching strategy without addressing these domain-specific challenges. Our method addressed these limitations by incorporating 3D-specific mechanisms that enable dataset distillation to effectively operate on point cloud data. We will revise the Related Work section in the camera-ready version to better reflect these critical connections between prior limitations and the design of our proposed method.

**Q2: Clarification on the experimental settings in Tables 5 and 6**

Let us clarify the experimental settings in Table 5 and Table 6. Whereas Table 5 presents an ablation study to evaluate the effectiveness of Semantic Alignment (SA) in our SADM loss, Table 6 analyzes the impact of synthetic dataset optimization and orientation optimization, with SA consistently applied in all cases. Specifically, we clarify the difference in terms of the optimization objectives. The optimization objective for 'w/ SA (proposed)' in Table 5 is formulated as
$$
	\\operatorname*{argmin}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}, \\boldsymbol{\\theta}} \\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{SADM}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}},  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}) \\quad \\text{where} \\quad  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}=\\mathcal{R}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}), \\tag{a}
$$
and that for `w/o SA' in Table 5 is
$$
\\operatorname*{argmin}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}, \\boldsymbol{\\theta}} \\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{MMD}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}},  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}) \\quad \\text{where} \\quad  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}=\\mathcal{R}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}),
$$
where the SADM loss is replaced with the standard MMD loss.
On the other hand, the optimization objective with '${\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}$' in Table 6 is 
$$
\\operatorname*{argmin}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}} \\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{SADM}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}},  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}),
$$
and that with '${\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}$' is 
$$
\\operatorname*{argmin}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}} \\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{SADM}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}},  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}). 
$$
The optimization objective with both '${\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}$' and '${\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}$' in Table 6 is the same to Equation (a).

**Q3: Generalizability and cross-dataset performance**

Figure 3 presents the qualitative results at PPC = 1, where only one synthetic sample represents the entire distribution of a certain class. In such an extreme case, it is natural to generate a smoothed shape (more generalized) to represent diverse shapes of samples in the class. However, as shown in Figure 7 in the supplementary material, our method gradually recovers more fine-grained details as PPC increases. 

We also evaluated the generalizability performance of the proposed method. In Table 2, we reported the cross-architecture generalization performance of the proposed method at PPC=3, where PointNet is used for dataset distillation and the resulting synthetic samples are evaluated on different backbone networks. Our method achieves the best performance across all architectures, demonstrating strong generalizability despite using the smoothed shapes of synthetic dataset. **Q1: Limitations of SADM loss**

We agree with the reviewer that the proposed SADM loss may not perfectly match semantically corresponding regions across diverse point cloud objects. However, our goal is not to achieve perfect matching but to improve the dataset distillation performance by matching the feature distributions more reliably. As shown in Table 5 in the supplementary material (below), our SADM-based feature sorting achieves significantly better performance compared with the unsorted setting and the other sorting strategies.

**Q2: Computational overhead**

Our method introduces additional computational overhead compared to the baseline DM, primarily due to the joint optimization of the synthetic point clouds and the rotation parameters. However, in this paper, we first introduced a new problem: 3D point cloud dataset distillation via distribution matching, and demonstrated the proposed method achieves significantly higher performance of dataset distillation compared with existing methods. To further justify the computational overhead, we conducted an experiment where DM was trained with its default setting, whereas the proposed method was trained during the same training time to DM. As shown below, even under the same training time, our method still significantly outperforms DM. We will discuss the computational overhead of the proposed method.

**Q3: Contribution**

Distribution matching (DM) is a widely used approach in numerous studies on dataset distillation. For example, various methods of image dataset distillation also have been developed based on DM, such as DataDAM [17] and M3D [26], and their contributions are improving the performance of DM with attention-based feature alignment or high-order distribution statistics. Moreover, as shown in Table 1 in the main paper and Table 4 in the supplimentary material, directly applying the dataset distillation methods for 2D images to the 3D point clouds, e.g., DM, DC, MTT, DataDAM, does not provide sufficient performance due to severely different characteristics between two domains. Considering the above, we are the first to explore the novel research area of dataset distillation for 3D point clouds via DM. Our contribution does not lie in the DM itself, but rather in proposing an efficient and reliable framework that jointly optimizes both the synthetic dataset and the rotational angles. By leveraging the unique properties of 3D point clouds, this framework is carefully designed to achieve substantially better performance than existing approaches.

We thank the reviewer to recognize the originality and significance of our paper. We respond to the reviewer's comments as follows.

**Q1: Feature channel**

For the $j$-th point ${\\bf p}\_j \in  \\mathbb{R}^{3}$ in a 3D point cloud object, a feature vector of $C$ features, 
$\\phi({\\bf p}\_j) = \\{ f\_{1,j}, f\_{2,j}, \\cdots, f\_{C,j} \\} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{C}$, is obtained by applying a randomly initialized feature extractor $\\phi$. Hence we have $C$ channels of features extracted from a 3D point cloud object ${\\bf p} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{3 \\times N}$ with $N$ points as
$$
	\\phi({\bf p}) = 
	\begin{bmatrix}
		f\_{1,1} & f\_{2,1} & \\cdots & f\_{C,1} \\\\
		f\_{1,2} & f\_{2,2} & \\cdots & f\_{C,2} \\\\
		\vdots & \vdots & \\ddots & \\vdots \\\\
		f\_{1,N} & f\_{2,N} & \\cdots & f\_{C,N}
	\end{bmatrix}
	= \\left[{\\bf f}\_1, {\\bf f}\_2, \\dots, {\\bf f}\_C\\right],
$$
where the $i$-th column ${\\bf f}\_i = \\{f\_{i,1}, f\_{i,2}, \\ldots, f\_{i,N} \\} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{N}$ means the vector of the $i$-th feature channel of $N$ points among $C$ channels. We will clarify this in the camera-ready.

**Q2: Learning of rotation angles**

During dataset distillation, the rotation angles $\\boldsymbol{\\theta}=(\\theta\_{x}, \\theta\_{y}, \\theta\_{z})$ are treated as learnable parameters which are jointly optimized with the synthetic dataset. At each iteration, the synthetic dataset $\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}$ is rotated by $\\mathcal{R}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}(\\cdot)$ to produce $\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}=\\mathcal{R}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}})$. The SADM loss $\\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{SADM}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}}, \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}})$ is then computed with $\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}$ and the real dataset $\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}}$. To minimize the loss, the gradients are back-propagated not only to $\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}$ but to $\\boldsymbol{\\theta}$ simultaneously, updating both the point coordinates of $\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}$ and the rotation angles $\\boldsymbol{\\theta}$. This joint optimization objective is fomulated as
$$
\\operatorname*{argmin}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}, \\boldsymbol{\\theta}} \\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{SADM}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{T}},  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}) \\quad \\text{where} \\quad  \\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}}=\\mathcal{R}\_{\\boldsymbol{\\theta}}(\\boldsymbol{\\mathcal{S}}).
$$
This will be clarified in the camera-ready.

**Q3: Comparison of KL divergence and MMD with Gaussian kernel**

Both of Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) are used to measure the distance between two distributions, but MMD is more proper in our framework since KLD is a parametric method requiring accurate probability density estimation. According to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have experimented with two experiments of Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) as alternatives to the MMD loss with a Gaussian kernel for measuring the discrepancy between the features. First, we followed the same setting as proposed method by measuring the discrepancy between the sorted features using KLD, after representing the feature distribution to the probability distribution using the softmax operation. We refer to this variant as Feature-KLD. Second, we adopted a knowledge distillation setup where the logits of the network, after being converted to probabilities, were used to compute the KLD loss between the original and synthetic datasets. This is denoted as Logits-KLD. As shown in the below table, the Feature-KLD approach yields significantly lower performance because the probability density estimation might be unreliable on high-dimensional and sparse feature space of 3D point clouds. Likewise, in Logits-KLD, the performance still results in low performance, because logits are highly compressed and lack the rich semantic information present in earlier feature maps. In addition, we also tested other kernel functions, including the linear and Laplacian kernels that show still less performance than the Gaussian kernel.

**Q4: Qualitative results for the guitar class**

The proposed method changes an initial sample to better represent the global distribution of the class. As shown in Figure 3, the proposed method largely changed the shape and orientation of the initial guitar sample (2nd row) into the last row, that reflects more diverse shapes and is more aligned with the dominant orientation of the diverse instances in the guitar class (1st row). In contrary, the existing methods generate almost same synthesized samples (3rd and 4th rows) to the initial sample, that fail to capture diverse shapes and representative orientation. Consequently, the proposed method optimizes more representative shape and orientation than the existing methods. To quantitatively evaluate the benefit of the proposed method, we compared the L2 distance between the class-wise averaged orientation of the samples in the original dataset and the orientation of the resulting synthetic samples obtained by DC[29], DM[28], and the propoised method, respectively. summary.value: This paper presents a distribution matching-based dataset distillation framework for 3D point clouds that introduces two key components: (1) a Semantically Aligned Distribution Matching (SADM) module to address misaligned semantic structures, where semantically similar regions across different 3D models are often associated with inconsistent point orders; (2) learnable rotation parameters (three rotation angles around the x, y, and z axes)  to estimate optimal orientations for synthetic data generation, which account for intra-class variability caused by different acquisition poses due to the absence of canonical orientation. SADM solves the optimization problem of aligning the feature distributions derived from the original and synthetic datasets by minimizing the SADM loss between features extracted by a randomly initialized, untrained network.  The authors conducted extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets to evaluate their framework, showing that the proposed method outperforms existing distillation approaches while maintaining strong cross-architecture generalization. Additionally, an ablation study was conducted to assess the effectiveness of the simultaneous optimization of both the geometric structure (semantic distribution matching) and the orientation of objects in the distilled dataset.

- Quality and Originality. The authors’ claims regarding the effectiveness of their dataset distillation method in addressing key limitations of existing approaches, namely, semantic misalignment and rotational variations, are well supported by the experimental results. summary.value: To address the issue of semantic misalignment in point clouds caused by their unordered nature, this paper introduces a Semantically Aligned Distribution Matching (SADM) loss function. It proposes a novel framework for 3D point cloud dataset distillation based on distribution matching, which simultaneously optimizes the geometric structure and orientation of the synthetic 3D objects.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

(1) Semantic Alignment via Feature Sorting: The method achieves semantic alignment by sorting the point feature values within each channel before computing the distance between two feature distributions.

(2) Robustness to Rotational Variance: To mitigate the issue of rotational variance, the framework jointly learns an optimal rotation angle during the update of the synthetic dataset, enabling a better alignment with the original feature distribution.

Weaknesses:

(1) Although the SADM loss enhances semantic consistency by sorting feature values, it cannot perfectly align semantically meaningful regions between different point cloud objects. This implies that in some cases, the semantic alignment may still be insufficiently accurate, thereby compromising the quality of the distilled dataset.

(2)  While the proposed method holds some advantages in training time over certain existing methods, its computational cost can still be high, especially for large-scale datasets or more complex 3D models. Furthermore, the joint optimization of the synthetic dataset and rotation parameters adds to the computational burden. Experimental data shows that its processing time is at least double that of the baseline Distribution Matching (DM) method.

(3) The SADM loss is designed to operate on sorted features within each channel to maintain semantic alignment. However, while the proposed method is effective for 3D point cloud dataset distillation, its core idea remains within the well-established distribution matching paradigm. The contribution is arguably an incremental improvement over existing distribution matching methods, and the work lacks a more fundamental insight or a novel approach to the distribution matching problem itself.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a distribution matching-based dataset distillation method for 3D point clouds. Most existing dataset distillation methods are designed for images, and the only existing method for point clouds overlooks the unordered and rotation-invariant nature of point clouds. To address these limitations, the paper:
+ Proposes Semantically Aligned Distribution Matching (SADM) method sorts the point features before performing distribution matching, resulting in preserved semantic structure. 
+ Directly optimizes for orientation to align the synthetic dataset and the original dataset more effectively.
Experiment results show that the proposed method outperforms baseline dataset distillation methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
$\\textbf{Strengths}$
+ This paper explored how to leverage the unique properties of point clouds to perform dataset distillation.
+ More sorting methods addressing the unordered nature of point clouds are tested, and results are given in Table 5 of appendix.
+ Experiment results show the proposed method improves over baselines.

$\\textbf{Major Weaknesses}$
+ All related works, including those on 3D point data analysis, coreset selection, and data distillation, are merely listed without in-depth discussion. The authors fail to analyze how these works are connected to the proposed method, rendering the related work section both overly lengthy and disconnected from the rest of the paper.
+ Concern about ablation study. In Table 5, the result of w/SA + MN40 is 72.08, which is consistent with the S+$\\theta$+Mixed (Mixed = MN40, see line 327) setting of Table 6, showing that **in Table 5, $\\theta$ orientation optimization is also used**. However, the w/oSA + MN40 result in Table 5 is 59.96, while the $\theta$ + Mixed result in Table 6 (row 2) is 62.17. This inconsistency should be clarified.
+ Figure 3 shows that the proposed method will cause relative large change of shape of point clouds, and loss of details / over-smoothing is also observed. Will the proposed cause degraded generalizability across datasets because of these behaviors? This should be explored.

$\\textbf{Minor Weaknesses}$
+ In line 168, should be 'descending order of their values' instead of 'descending order of their sizes'.
+ In line 179, should be 'largest' instead of 'most largest'.
+ The results in Table 5 of the appendix are important and should be placed in the main text.
+ Table 5 and Table 6 are highly redundant and can be considered to be merged to together.
+ Proposition 1 is quite obvious and does not need a large space in the main text.

questions.value:
1. Please refine the related work section to connect the related works to the proposed method.
2. Please clarify the inconsistency between Table 5 and Table 6.
3. Can you provide cross-dataset performance if possible?

The authors have addressed my concerns on the evaluation protocol and potential harm to cross-dataset generalization capability of the proposed method.

Although the related work part of this paper is not well organized, failing to give a good background to the readers, given that data distillation of point cloud data is less researched and the proposed method have relative good performance, I will suggest a borderline accept to this paper.

summary.value: The paper presents a dataset distillation method that explores distribution matching for distillation of 3D point clouds. The method jointly optimizes the geometric structures and the orientations of the synthetic 3D objects. It introduces a Semantically Aligned Distribution Matching loss that sorts point features to address the semantic misalignment caused by unordered points, In addition, it learn the optimal rotation angles to better align with the original feature distribution to address the rotation variation. Experiments show promising results.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength
1. The work addresses a relatively new problem of dataset distillation of point clouds.
2. The work presents a method that address the unordered point features and rotation issue with promising performance.

Weakness
1. The significance of the proposed method is not clear. The motivation of the work is to suppress datasets without sacrificing useful information. On the other hand, the second point is not well discussed and reflected in the experiment part. 
2. The experimentation is not convincing. The comparison involves a single point cloud dataset distillation method only, and the method just applies one existing image dataset distillation method that uses gradient matching. However, there are many other image dataset distillation methods that use trajectory matching, distribution matching, etc. The experiments should include comparisons with other image dataset distillation methods that apply to point cloud dataset distillation.
3. The experiments are not clear. Take Table 1 as an example. What does the row 'whole' mean? Is it the performance using the original dataset? If so, the performance of the proposed distillation method drops sharply especially for the natural data, instead of without sacrificing much useful information. In addition, the meaning of the row 'Ratio' is not explained clearly either. Further, the text mentions comparison with PPC [27] in Table 1 but I don't see the comparison there. 
4. The unclarity applies to other experimental results as well. For example, DC performs better than DM for synthetic data but worse than DM for real data consistently, why? In addition, why does the proposed method improves less on the natural point clouds?

questions.value:

The experiments should include comparisons with other image dataset distillation methods like trajectory matching and distribution matching that apply to point cloud dataset distillation.

3. Why does DC perform better than DM for synthetic data but worse than DM for real data consistently? Why does the proposed method improves less on the natural point clouds?

title.value: Dataset Distillation of 3D Point Clouds via Distribution Matching

abstract.value: Large-scale datasets are usually required to train deep neural networks; however, they increase computational complexity, hindering practical applications. Recently, dataset distillation for images and texts has attracted considerable attention, as it reduces the original dataset to a small synthetic one to alleviate the computational burden of training while preserving essential task-relevant information. However, dataset distillation for 3D point clouds remains largely unexplored, as point clouds exhibit fundamentally different characteristics from those of images, making this task more challenging. In this paper, we propose a distribution-matching-based distillation framework for 3D point clouds that jointly optimizes the geometric structures and orientations of synthetic 3D objects. To address the semantic misalignment caused by the unordered nature of point clouds, we introduce a Semantically Aligned Distribution Matching (SADM) loss, which is computed on the sorted features within each channel. Moreover, to handle rotational variations, we jointly learn optimal rotation angles while updating the synthetic dataset to better align with the original feature distribution. Extensive experiments on widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing dataset distillation approaches, achieving higher accuracy and strong cross-architecture generalization.
